title: Occasion and publication
short: Written in April 1860 after Longfellow climbed the Old North Church tower; printed in the Atlantic Monthly, January 1861, and later as 'The Landlord's Tale'.
body: Longfellow visited the Old North Church on 5 April 1860 and began the poem the next day. It appeared in the January 1861 Atlantic Monthly (issued 20 December 1860) and was reprinted in the Boston Evening Transcript; in Tales of a Wayside Inn (1863) it became 'The Landlord's Tale', the first story told by guests at the Wayside Inn in Sudbury. The storyteller's opening address to 'my children' frames the poem as oral tradition passed down the generations, which is exactly the national memory it set out to create. The poem made Revere a national hero: his 1818 obituary had not even mentioned the ride.

anchor: Hardly a man is now alive
title: 'Hardly a man is now alive'
short: Eighty-five years after 1775, the last eyewitnesses were gone: the poem marks the moment history passes into legend.
body: The claim was nearly literal: Jonathan Harrington, the fifer at Lexington, the last survivor of the battle on the green, died in 1854. With living memory ending, the speaker takes on the task of transmission. The line also concedes, quietly, that what follows is not eyewitness testimony but a retelling, a point relevant to the poem's famous historical liberties. Longfellow knew he was making legend, and historians such as Fischer have shown how much of Revere's popular image derives from this poem rather than from the documents.

anchor: the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five
title: 18 April 1775
short: The night of 18-19 April 1775, when British troops marched from Boston to seize colonial military stores at Concord.
body: General Thomas Gage sent some 700 regulars under Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith to destroy arms and powder stored at Concord, and Boston's patriots, warned of the plan, sent riders to alert the countryside and the leaders Samuel Adams and John Hancock at Lexington. The fighting at Lexington and Concord on 19 April began the American War of Independence. 'Seventy-five' is the colloquial way of naming the year, as of a date everyone knows.

sources.cite: David Hackett Fischer, Paul Revere's Ride (Oxford UP, 1994)

title: 'One, if by land, and two, if by sea'
short: The poem's most famous line reverses history: Revere arranged the signal for patriots in Charlestown; he did not wait for it.
body: In fact Revere, already knowing the route, asked that lanterns be shown in the steeple to warn patriots across the river in Charlestown in case he could not get out of Boston; two lanterns meant that the troops would cross the Charles by boat ('by sea') rather than march out over Boston Neck ('by land'). The 'friend' who hung them was probably Robert Newman, sexton of Christ Church. Longfellow made Revere the receiver of the signal so that the climactic moment could be his. Revere's own account to Jeremy Belknap describes the arrangement.

title: muffled oar
short: Oars wrapped in cloth at the oarlocks to deaden sound; in reality two friends rowed Revere across.
body: To 'muffle' oars is to wrap them where they rest in the rowlocks so that they make no noise (OED). Revere did not row himself: two companions rowed him from the North End across the Charles to Charlestown, past a British warship. Longfellow's single hero, rowing silently, is again a concentration of a collective effort into one figure. Muffling itself is true to the night: secrecy and silence were essential, since the boat had to pass close to a British warship.

title: the Somerset
short: HMS Somerset, a 64-gun ship of the line anchored in the Charles River to guard the crossing; Revere slipped past her in the dark.
body: The Somerset was a large Royal Navy warship (a 'man-of-war') stationed between Boston and Charlestown. Longfellow turns her into a Gothic image: a 'phantom ship', her masts 'like a prison bar' across the moon, a black hulk magnified by its reflection. The prison image makes British power a jailer of the colony. Historically the moon had risen and the boat passed close to the ship without being challenged.

anchor: the measured tread of the grenadiers
title: grenadiers
short: Elite infantry, originally soldiers who threw grenades; here the grenadier companies of the British regiments in Boston.
body: By 1775 grenadiers were the tall picked men of each British regiment, chosen for strength rather than for throwing grenades. Gage's expedition was made up of the grenadier and light infantry companies drawn from several regiments, which were assembled on Boston Common and taken across the Back Bay in boats. The poem's 'muster', 'sound of arms' and 'measured tread' build suspense by sound.

title: the Old North Church
short: Christ Church in Boston's North End (1723), the city's oldest surviving church building.
body: Christ Church, now called Old North, was an Anglican church whose steeple was visible across the harbour to Charlestown, which is why it was chosen for the signal. The poem made the church a shrine: and a granite tablet commemorating the signal lanterns was added to its facade in 1878. Longfellow's visit to the tower in April 1860 is the likely source of the climb, with its startled pigeons, sombre rafters and 'trembling ladder'.

anchor: in the churchyard, lay the dead
title: the dead in their night-encampment
short: The graves on the hill are an army sleeping in tents, and the wind is a sentinel saying 'All is well!'
body: Below the church lies Copp's Hill Burying Ground, where early Bostonians are buried. Longfellow extends a military conceit: the dead are encamped on the hill, the graves are tents, and the night-wind 'creeping along from tent to tent' plays sentinel, whispering the watchman's call 'All is well!'. The passage pauses the action for a moment of eerie stillness and links the coming fight to the ancestral dead, a typical Longfellow move from narrative into meditation.

title: a bridge of boats
short: The line of British boats crossing the Charles seems to make a floating bridge.
body: A bridge of boats is a pontoon bridge, a military bridge of boats lashed side by side; the dark line on the tide is the flotilla carrying the troops across the Back Bay toward Cambridge. The simile is the moment of recognition: the troops are going 'by sea', so two lanterns must be hung. The image also continues the poem's pattern of seeing danger as shapes in the dark, a 'shadowy something far away', before it is identified.

anchor: A second lamp in the belfry
title: Suspense and tense
short: The poem shifts between past and present tense and holds the second lantern back to the end of the stanza.
body: Longfellow alternates the narrative past ('Then he climbed') with the dramatic present ('he looks', 'He springs'), so the climax happens before the reader's eyes. The stanza delays: Revere 'lingers and gazes' after the first glimmer until the second lamp appears. Critics note the poem's cinematic intercutting between the friend in the tower and Revere on the shore. The repeated 'Meanwhile' marks the cross-cutting. Revere's impatience (he pats his horse, stamps, tightens the girth) is rendered in a quick list of actions while he waits.

title: The galloping metre
short: Four-beat lines with many triple (anapaestic) feet, in rhyming couplets and triplets, are often heard as imitating the horse's gallop.
body: The metre is basically a four-stress line in which two unstressed syllables often fall between stresses ('a HURry of HOOFS in a VILLage STREET'), so the rhythm runs like hoofbeats. Rhymes come in couplets and clusters rather than fixed stanzas, and the stanzas vary in length with the action. Readers have long heard the gallop in the cadence, and the strong rhythm made the poem a classroom recitation piece for over a century.

title: The spark and the nation
short: A spark struck from the pebbles by the horse's shoe kindles the whole land: an image of revolution from a tiny cause.
body: The image is double: a literal spark from iron on stone, and the 'spark' of rebellion that sets the country ablaze. 'The fate of a nation' shows Longfellow's purpose, to make a founding myth. Writing in 1860, as the Union was splitting over slavery, Longfellow could expect readers to hear another nation's fate in the balance. The repetition of 'spark struck out by that steed' within four lines insists on the image, and the alliteration of 'flying fearless and fleet' speeds the line.

title: the Mystic ... Medford town
short: The Mystic River, which Revere crossed on the road from Charlestown through Medford.
body: After a British patrol blocked the direct road, Revere rode by a northern route through Medford, crossing the Mystic River, and alarmed the captain of the Medford minutemen before turning west to Lexington. The name, from an Algonquian word for a large tidal river, is a gift to the poem's atmosphere. The stanza slows: 'tranquil and broad and deep', with hooves 'now soft on the sand, now loud on the ledge', a contrast of silence and noise that runs through the whole poem.

title: The clock refrain
short: Twelve, one, two: a striking clock refrain marks the ride, though Longfellow stretches its timetable and its route.
body: The refrain gives the ride a ritual structure (Medford at twelve, Lexington at one, Concord at two), each with its own village sounds. In fact Revere reached Lexington around midnight, and he never reached Concord: after leaving Lexington with William Dawes and Samuel Prescott he was captured by a British patrol; only Prescott got through to Concord. Modern critics regularly point to these liberties, and Fischer's history documents the real ride in detail.

anchor: the meeting-house windows, blank and bare
title: the meeting-house windows
short: The Lexington meeting-house seems to stare in horror at the killing that will happen on the green beside it at dawn.
body: A New England 'meeting-house' was the Congregational church, used also for town meetings. The personification ('Gaze at him with a spectral glare') anticipates the morning, when eight militiamen were killed on Lexington Green, in front of the meeting-house. Prolepsis, the foreshadowing of future events in the narrative present, is the stanza's device. The weathercock that 'swims' in the moonlight is a precise detail of the gilded vane, and the windows are 'blank and bare' like the eyes of the dead.

title: the bridge in Concord
short: The North Bridge at Concord, where the first British volley killed militiamen; the sleeper 'first to fall' recalls Captain Isaac Davis of Acton.
body: At the North Bridge on the morning of 19 April the British fired on the advancing militia, killing Captain Isaac Davis of the Acton minutemen and Abner Hosmer, and the militia's return fire was the 'shot heard round the world' of Emerson's 'Concord Hymn' (1837). Longfellow's sleeper who will be 'first to fall' is generic, but the details fit Davis. The tender image of the man 'safe and asleep in his bed' heightens the pathos of the morning.

title: 'You know the rest'
short: The narrator skips the battle: the British retreat to Boston under fire from militia behind walls and fences.
body: The phrase assumes a shared national story: the British 'fired and fled', and the militia harried them all the way back to Charlestown, firing 'ball for ball' from behind fences and stone walls. The retreat cost the British about 270 casualties. Longfellow's picture of farmers fighting from cover became the standard image of the minuteman. The brisk summary, after the long build-up, shows where Longfellow's interest lay: in the warning and the waking of the people rather than in the fighting. 'The books you have read' assigns the battle to history, the ride to poetry.

sources.cite: David Hackett Fischer, Paul Revere's Ride (Oxford UP, 1994)

title: The poem's purpose in 1860
short: The closing prophecy speaks to Longfellow's present: on the eve of the Civil War, the nation must waken again.
body: Longfellow, an opponent of slavery since Poems on Slavery (1842), published the poem weeks after Lincoln's election and as South Carolina was voting to secede (20 December 1860). 'The hour of darkness and peril and need' points beyond 1775 to the crisis of the Union. Jill Lepore has argued that the poem is in an important sense about slavery and John Brown, whose raid and execution (1859) Longfellow noted in his journal; others read it as a call to unity rather than to arms. The 'night-wind of the Past' makes history a living voice that 'shall echo forevermore'.
